title: I created a game for my nephews
author: blc365
selftext:
So I work in IT for a living but am in no way a game developer or even really work with code on a daily basis. That being said, I’ve always been interested in game development. One day after watching some of the games my nephews were playing, I decided to see if I could leverage Claude to make something better that we could play together. I wanted to make it inspired by flappy bird as I loved the simplicity and the competitiveness back when it was around. i know there is no shortage of flappy bird clones but I didn’t want to just make a clone, I had a lot of ideas to increase the competitive side of it and take the pipe flyer to a new level. It took me about 3 months of development, play testing, and rebuilding until it hit a state I was happy with. 

Some of the things I learned along the way - 

Absolutely do not have any expectation that the AI will get it right the first time. There have been many things in the game that I had to tweak, playtest, tweak, playtest, and tweak some more. Sometimes I could never get something right and had to scratch it. Other times, I had to go out and do research over the best practices for what the task was I was doing and learn it myself so that I could articulate what I was needing. There are a surprising amount of complex mechanics, even in a simple game.

While you can API into most other sites you’d need, I would say it’s beneficial for you to set up your servers / OAuth / cloud needs to understand your full infrastructure. This of course varies by how and what you’re making. With mine being a mobile app, I used Supabase for my data retention needs and found it very beneficial that I set it up on my own for troubleshooting later. 

I got bit in the butt more than once by a chat suddenly becoming full and locking up - have your chat make and maintain a living handoff doc that details everything you do and what you are planning to do. This makes a sudden locked chat not nearly as taxing and the new chat can pick right up where you left off. Establish an update process so it updates it after every change.

Having a couple quality play testers goes a long way. I had Claude do checks all the time for bugs but it doesn’t catch everything and it’s hard as an individual to always verify every little thing. Multiple times a couple dedicated play testers I had caught things before I did. 

When making a mobile game you plan to release on iOS and Google Play, you realize they can have a lot of different requirements and you need to build your game in a way that can support both of them but not step on each other. Apple in particular doesn’t like to see pretty much anything mentioning Google on their side. But you don’t want to make two different game versions that have to be kept up with because you’ll eventually end up with drift. Just add an OS filter so you can tell which one you’re on and dish the appropriate fields for what that returns. 

All in all, i really enjoyed creating this game. I don’t know if I’ll make anymore but I do plan to keep adding to Neon Drift Arcade as I come up with other ideas I think would be fun or enhance the game. 

Check out my website for more information I’ve created about it and you can play the game browser side or get it on Apple App Store or Google Play Store. Also feel free to DM with any questions!

[Neon Drift Arcade](https://www.neondriftgame.com)

replies.author: blc365
replies.body: The classic mode is pretty much that, but I’ve added a daily challenge also, a storm mode which is projectiles, a versus mode to challenge friends, and a last pilot standing mode which is a 2-10 player last man standing race. All of which have their own leaderboards and unlocks.
